cases.working_notes: Keep the conditional denoising result separate from the discrete-rotation implementation. Use the shared RGB backbone comparison to avoid attributing all simulation gains to additional 3D observations, and the matched voxel hardware baseline to test an architectural contribution. Simulation reports training maxima, not final-checkpoint success. Request uncertainty on the task averages and numerical results of the referenced component ablation before quantifying separate contributions of voxel input and equivariance. The 200-versus-1,000-demonstration comparison is descriptive and averages across tasks; it does not establish uniform taskwise superiority.
cases.abstract: We present Equivariant Diffusion Policy, a behavior-cloning method that couples planar scene rotations to six-degree-of-freedom gripper actions throughout denoising. When the expert policy is SO(2)-equivariant and noise transforms like actions, the associated noise predictor inherits that equivariance. We derive rotation representations for absolute and relative pose control, whose transformations differ by left multiplication versus conjugation. Equivariant encoders and a decoder surround a temporal U-Net shared across discrete rotation-indexed embeddings, imposing this structure without replacing the temporal backbone. Image and voxel observations provide two implementations; voxel rotations align with state rotations, whereas oblique camera images introduce a symmetry mismatch. On 12 MimicGen tasks, the RGB version reaches 53.7% average peak success with 100 demonstrations per task under absolute control, versus 42.0% for a non-equivariant diffusion policy using the same temporal backbone. The voxel version reaches 72.6% with 200 demonstrations, compared with 71.4% for that RGB baseline with 1,000. Physical experiments compare policies using the same voxel input and approximately matched parameter counts: the equivariant policy achieves 80-95% success across six tasks with 20-60 demonstrations. These results support rotation-structured denoising for data-limited manipulation.
cases.results: With RGB observations and a temporal U-Net backbone shared by EquiDiff (Im) and DiffPo-C, absolute-control success averages 53.7% versus 42.0% at 100 demonstrations per task across 12 MimicGen environments. These values average, over three seeds, the maximum success rate among 50 evaluations during training. The comparison shows that the low-data gain does not require changing to voxel observations. Control mode matters: at the same demonstration budget, RGB relative-control averages are 35.4% and 33.3%. On hardware, both methods instead receive the same voxel grid, and the non-equivariant baseline has approximately matched trainable parameter counts. With 40 demonstrations, letter alignment succeeds in 19/20 trials for EquiDiff versus 0/20 for the baseline. Bagel baking, trained with 58 demonstrations, succeeds in 16/20 versus 2/20 trials; all EquiDiff failures on that task are attributed to robot joint limits. Together, these comparisons support a benefit from the equivariant architecture beyond voxel input alone, while showing that performance depends on control mode and execution constraints.

cases.abstract: Re-Mix curates robot demonstration mixtures without selecting data for a known target task. It learns reusable domain weights through minimax optimization of excess imitation loss relative to a reference policy, so weighting depends on the gap to a reference rather than raw domain difficulty. Applying this objective to heterogeneous robot data requires more than importing robust optimization: action scales differ across controllers, continuous losses are sensitive to outliers and multimodal actions, and reference models can memorize limited demonstrations. Re-Mix applies Gaussian action normalization within embodiments, discretizes actions for weight estimation, and selects checkpoints before domain-level overfitting. The resulting weights are reused to train diffusion policies independently of the discrete curation model. Real-robot experiments on RT-X and Bridge V2 use 25 in-domain demonstrations for each of three tasks at a 5% co-training weight. With 25% of RT-X retained, Re-Mix achieves 80% mean success, compared with 38% for uniform and 33% for human-curated weights. Full Bridge training shows little benefit from reweighting, whereas subsetting exposes substantial differences. The findings support learned mixture weights for selective data reduction, with their benefit depending on dataset composition and training regime.
cases.results: At the same 25% data-retention budget, Re-Mix yields higher reported mean success than alternative curation strategies: 80% versus 38% with uniform and 33% with human-defined weights on RT-X, and 90% versus 50% with uniform and 22% with vision-based SSP on Bridge. Each subset comparison covers four tasks with ten real-robot trials per task. Final diffusion policies train for 400,000 gradient steps and include 25 in-domain demonstrations for each of three representative tasks at a 5% mixture weight; the evaluation tasks test shifts beyond this co-training data. These comparisons show that the composition of a reduced training set matters, rather than data volume alone. In contrast, full Bridge training shows similar performance under Re-Mix and uniform weighting on its two evaluated tasks. The subset ablations further report worse outcomes with continuous-action weight estimation or an overfit reference checkpoint, supporting the discretization and early-stopping choices without identifying either as the sole source of improvement.
